title: The Warning I Saw in Diotrephes Loving First Place
paragraphs:
The Warning I Saw in Diotrephes Loving First Place
The Quiet Sin That Can Destroy a Church Before Anyone Notices—And the Grace That Still Calls Us Home
There are sins that shock the world.
Then there are sins that quietly destroy the Church.

Not through violence.
Not through false miracles.
Not through open rebellion.
But through one dangerous desire...
The need to be first.
It rarely begins with hatred.
It usually begins with recognition.

Someone thanks you.
People begin listening to you.
Your opinions carry weight.
Your influence grows.
Your name becomes familiar.
Then, almost unnoticed, your heart slowly starts craving something it was never created to hold.
Not Christ's glory.
Your own.

That is why one of the shortest books in the New Testament contains one of the strongest warnings for every pastor, ministry leader, volunteer, content creator, Bible teacher, church member, and even every ordinary believer who has ever desired to be noticed.
Hidden inside 3 John is a man whose name most Christians barely remember.
Yet his story continues to repeat itself every single day.
His name was Diotrephes.
And if we are honest...
There is a little bit of Diotrephes hiding inside every sinful heart.
The Apostle John writes:
— 3 John 9 (KJV)
The phrase "loveth to have the preeminence" deserves careful attention because the Holy Spirit chose every word intentionally.
In the Greek text, it is:
φιλοπρωτεύων (philoprōteuōn)
It is a compound word.
φιλέω (phileō) means "to love," "to cherish," or "to delight in."
πρῶτος (prōtos) means "first," "chief," or "highest."
Together they paint a terrifying picture.
Not someone who occasionally leads.
Not someone who simply holds responsibility.
But someone who loves being first.
Someone whose identity has become wrapped around prominence.
Someone who secretly believes the work of God revolves around themselves.
John never accuses Diotrephes of adultery.
He never accuses him of stealing.
He never says he denied Christ.
Instead...
His greatest sin was loving the position that belonged only to Jesus.
That should stop every one of us.
Because Scripture never says Christ merely occupies first place.
He is first place.
Paul writes:
— Colossians 1:18 (KJV)
The Greek word here is closely related:
πρωτεύων (prōteuōn)
Christ alone possesses supreme place.
The tragedy is heartbreaking.
Diotrephes desired for himself what belonged exclusively to Christ.
That has been humanity's oldest temptation.
In the Garden of Eden, the serpent whispered,
"You shall be as God."
Not merely knowing good and evil.
But becoming the center.
Lucifer fell because he said,
"I will exalt my throne."
Babel was built because mankind wanted to make a name for themselves.
King Saul feared David's popularity more than he feared God.
The Pharisees loved the best seats.
Even the disciples argued about who would be greatest while Jesus walked toward the Cross.
The sin keeps changing clothes.
But it never changes its heart.
Today it hides behind ministry titles.
Social media numbers.
Church platforms.
Podcast downloads.
Book sales.
Conference invitations.
Followers.
Recognition.
Influence.
Applause.
Verification badges.
Sometimes we don't even notice when serving Christ quietly transforms into building our own kingdom.
That is why John's warning feels almost painfully modern.
He continues describing Diotrephes:

"...prating against us with malicious words..."
— 3 John 10 (KJV)
The Greek expression carries the idea of speaking nonsense, empty accusations, or malicious chatter.
Pride always protects itself.
When someone loves being first, anyone who threatens that position becomes an enemy.
Truth becomes secondary.
Reputation becomes everything.

Eventually Diotrephes refused to welcome faithful believers and even expelled others from the church for showing hospitality (3 John 10). The one who wanted to lead God's people had become a gatekeeper against God's servants.
What began as a love for prominence ended in division.
That is the nature of pride.
It never stays private.
It spreads.
Yet Scripture does not leave us with Diotrephes as the final word.
Because the gospel never ends with scandal.
It ends with grace.
Jesus Christ, the One who truly deserved first place, did the opposite of Diotrephes.
The eternal Son of God possessed every right to glory, honor, worship, and authority, yet He humbled Himself.
Paul writes:
— Philippians 2:5–7 (KJV)

The Greek phrase ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσεν (heauton ekenōsen) means "He emptied Himself." This does not mean Christ ceased to be God. Rather, He willingly laid aside the privileges of His divine glory, taking the form of a servant without surrendering His divine nature. He humbled Himself in obedience to the Father, demonstrating perfect love rather than self-exaltation.
Where Diotrephes grasped for honor, Christ released it.
Where Diotrephes rejected faithful believers, Jesus welcomed sinners.
Where Diotrephes pushed others away, Jesus stretched out His hands on a Roman cross.
Where Diotrephes sought a throne without a cross, Jesus embraced the cross before receiving the throne.
That is why our ministry theme is more than a slogan.

Every one of us has battled the temptation to be noticed, praised, or preferred. The gospel does not excuse that pride, but it exposes it so that it can be crucified with Christ. The answer is not pretending we are humble; it is continually surrendering our hearts to the One who alone deserves first place.
Perhaps today the Holy Spirit is not asking whether you attend church, teach the Bible, preach sermons, create Christian content, or lead a ministry.
Perhaps He is asking a far deeper question:
Who truly holds first place in your heart?
If this message has uncovered something you have quietly struggled with, don't hide it. Bring it into the light where grace heals what pride destroys.

You never know who is silently wrestling with pride, recognition, or the temptation to build their own kingdom instead of Christ's. Sometimes one shared message becomes the turning point in another person's walk with God.
They may need the encouragement that the Lord sees every unseen act of obedience.
We all need reminders that Jesus alone deserves the preeminence.
Because in the end, history will not remember who insisted on sitting in the highest seat.
Heaven will remember those who knelt lowest at the feet of Jesus.
